Everyone is a unique situation, with unique potential. First things you need to do all involve posture. Its extremely difficult to assess yourself, as we lack knowledge, and all want to be good and protect ourselves from inward harsh criticism (this is healthy and normal, but if you can go for it, be aware the bias is invisible.) You need to get amazing erect posture. You need superior reflexive action of the rotator cuff. Your ankles and feet need to work very well. Beyond just this, then you need to develop a spine that arches and flexes like a gymnasts.

I would go ahead and say I like Foundation 1, which I do, but Handstand 1 is a much better beginner routine to go with postural adjustments. F1's first level progressions are a great indicator if you are prepared for greater gymnastic endeavors, and the exercises are extremely well chosen, but they are not corrective on their own.

H1 on the other hand, is pretty much the same as what you'll see from martial arts instructors around the world, but without aforementioned postural strong spine, hips and reflexive rotator cuff and shoulder girdle, finding correct form in wrist push-ups and a tripod headstand will be difficult on your own.

There are many ways to skin a cat, but Gray Cook's "Secret of the Shoulder" is a great place to start, and offers simple assessments for the 4 quarters of your body, as without a properly functioning spine the shoulder is going to be limited.

Paul Chek's "Scientific Back Training" is a good video which dares try and help plebs train their own backs to basic postural function. I'm sure there are many others out their who also try, but this is one I've used and I think you'll find the way he talks prophetic of what Gray and hundreds of others go on about now.

Rolling assessments are great, lots on youtube about this.

But I'll cut this rant short. You have an entire body to consider, and the fact of the matter is Ido Portal and Coach Sommers are the guys who have had some success in training adults in in gymnastics, and willing to talk about it somewhat publicly. I do not think you can just start their training without first doing basic work on posture, as they do not provide that in their material (although I imagine they know something about it in person, its just too specific to make a program out of.) Once you are at the bottom of the mountain, F1 is a good place to start with progressions, but you'll definitely want to diversify on top of that, as people having the greatest success with it trained with Mr.Sommers himself, or were already superb, mobile athletes who benefited from a new routine. We all benefit from switching it up, it gives a chance to change the way you move.
